groups.title: Pace of aging
groups.description: The test, the gauge, and what the result means.

slides.title: The test
slides.notes: The test I and many aging scientists settled on: DunedinPACE. It estimates the speed your body is aging. 1.0 means one year per calendar year. My best score was 0.65; the average of my three tests is 0.665. So I age about 6.5 years while the typical person ages 10. Built at Duke and Columbia from the Dunedin, New Zealand cohort followed since birth; published 2022; used in 65+ large studies in 18 countries. Nature Aging 2024: faster pace predicted shorter healthspans and lives. The part ads leave out: my score went back up to 0.76 after supplement mistakes and a chaotic menopausal stretch. Testing again at year end. One test, one person, one body: a story, not a clinical trial.

slides.title: The icing
slides.notes: Why start with the icing? Because it is everywhere and makes people feel behind. Affordable on the left: sauna, prebiotics, most supplements. Real money as you move right: NAD drips, peptides, stem cells, hyperbaric oxygen, rapamycin. At the far end a program costing about two million dollars a year with a medical team and blood transfusions. I am not saying don’t. I am saying not first. Nobody in the blue zones is in a hyperbaric chamber. What I do: a tested longevity supplement combination and sauna three to five days a week; the sauna is what gets me out of bed. Finnish data 2024: 2,575 men, 28 years; four to seven sessions a week, about 40 percent lower all-cause mortality than once a week. The coin on the far left is me: twelve dollars a day.

slides.title: Same bedtime, every day.
slides.notes: Archived r4 v1; source filename v1-07.jpg.

slides.title: Sleep
slides.notes: Bottom of the cake: sleep, the night shift. Your brain has a drainage system that flushes the day’s waste, mostly while you sleep: the glymphatic system, imaged in living people for the first time by OHSU in 2024. No middle-of-the-night shame spirals; I have had insomnia. Focus on what we control: timing and routine. 2023, 60,000-plus adults: sleep regularity predicted lifespan better than duration; the most regular sleepers had up to 48 percent lower mortality risk. My routine: last meal three hours before bed, ten-minute walk, screens off an hour before, brush, floss, wash, eye mask, cool room. Target window 9 PM to 5 AM. Borrow the order and the consistency, not my clock.

slides.title: Quote
slides.notes: For anyone who lives by this line: you will die much earlier by it as well. I used to admire it. Then I started testing. The fastest way to speed up your pace is neglecting sleep. Be consistent. Everything else we cover tonight will help your sleep inside that window.

groups.title: Same age, different healthspan
groups.description: The contrast that leads into movement.

slides.title: Same age
slides.notes: Third layer: movement. One picture of why it matters: two people, the same age in calendar years. One strong, one on a walker. Mayo Clinic, December 2024, 183 countries: the gap between how long we live and how long we live in good health. Worldwide 9.6 years. United States 12.4 years, the widest gap in the world. I am in the middle of this with my parents: a decade of not getting to the store or the bathroom alone, losing email and the phone, forgetting finances and grandchildren, falling at night. Not everything is escapable. But exercise is the single most powerful intervention we have. Can we shrink that window to almost nothing? What movement?

slides.title: Movement week
slides.notes: That is what my week looks like. How do you fit all this in? I did not build it in a day: twenty-five years of adding, subtracting and fine-tuning. Travel and deadlines change it, but the bones stay. It is an example of a diversified portfolio, not a test to pass tomorrow. Start small: short movement breaks, a few sets of air squats through the day, cut post-meal glucose spikes by over twenty percent; big leg muscles pull glucose straight out of the blood. A daily walk and air squats while the coffee brews is a very respectable start. Check with your doctor if you need to. The goal is to start moving.

groups.title: Stress: the layer people skip
groups.description: The stress layer and the response over time.

slides.title: Stress
slides.notes: The fourth layer is the one almost everyone skips. I hate the phrase stress management; it sounds like an HR seminar. But stress is the silent saboteur: pristine diet, all the weights, 7,000 steps, and elevated cortisol undoes it from the inside. 2018, a stressful divorce: my cortisol curve was inverted, rock bottom in the morning, spiking at night. Supplements are a band-aid. I learned Transcendental Meditation; six months later the curve had normalized and has stayed that way. TM is not magic; breathwork, mindfulness, prayer, meditation all trigger the same reset. The best practice is the one you will do. Free five-minute tool: the physiological sigh, Stanford: five minutes a day improved mood and calmed the nervous system faster than standard meditation. Double inhale through the nose, long slow exhale through the mouth. Three together, now.

groups.title: The daily protocol
groups.description: Choose the complete day view, ring, or timeline.

slides.title: The protocol
slides.notes: All four layers in a single day, so you can see where they fight for the same hour. 5 AM wake, water, prayer, light. 7 AM movement and sauna. 8 AM eating window opens: greens, protein, fiber, fruit. 9 AM caffeine cut-off. Eating window 8 to 6, ten hours: constraining eating to 8 to 10 hours improved blood sugar and body fat without changing what people ate; earlier windows do even better. Midday main meal and a walk. 1 PM stress reset. 6 PM kitchen closes, three hours before bed. 8 PM screens off. 9 PM lights out. Notice: the whole day is built backward from bedtime. Lights out at nine sets dinner at six; dinner at six sets the window opening at eight. Sleep is the master foundation. Life wins sometimes; I reset the next morning. What transfers is the order of operations: sleep, then food, movement, stress. My 5 AM might be your 6:30. Screenshot this slide and pick one or two anchors.

slides.title: Three questions
slides.notes: That is the cake. Numbers are not what kept me showing up for twenty-five years. Three questions did. Intention: the sentence on the wall. Mine: I want my healthspan to match my lifespan; drag the second line up to meet the first. Why: the feeling behind it, the engine that keeps you going when protocols become routine. Mine: being here to show my son a different possibility for how we age, and keeping Parkinson’s and dementia far away. Resources: time, energy, money, relationships, the real amounts. Mine: about an hour in the morning and twelve dollars a day. Resources filter out the adverts. No million-dollar budget? Great: let go of peptides and stem cells and focus on a solid gym routine. Friends who want this too? Start a group. When all three align you stop asking what should I do and start asking does this fit. A sauna session fits. A 9 PM bedtime fits. Not willpower: three honest questions doing the heavy lifting.
